activities.anchor: Slide the frequency and count the cycles
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the one universal interval
activities.name: smOctaveCloze

config.text: A clean %%0%% is the %%1%% — the only interval every musical culture on Earth treats as 'the same note, higher': 440 and %%2%% Hz are both 'A'.
config.hint: The grey companion wave completes exactly two cycles for your one — and doubling the frequency names the interval.

activities.anchor: a taller wave is a higher note
activities.caption: file each change under the dial that made it
activities.name: smWaveBuckets

config.prompt: Pitch and loudness are independent dials — file each change:

items.label: the note climbs without getting louder
the eardrum is pushed 440 times a second
the sound gets louder at the same pitch

config.why: The two properties live in different dimensions of the same wave — raise the amplitude and the note does not move; raise the frequency and it climbs without getting louder.

activities.caption: pair each consonant interval with its ratio
activities.name: smRatioMatch

config.prompt: The strong shared preference — pair each interval with the ratio Pythagoras found:
config.why: Simple frequency ratios sound good to human ears — the foundation Western music is built on, attributed to Pythagoras experimenting with stretched strings around 550 BCE.

activities.anchor: Here is a problem Pythagoras left unsolved
activities.caption: put the tempered fifth on the cents scale
activities.name: smFifthPlace

config.prompt: A pure fifth is 702 cents (100 cents = one semitone). Equal temperament flattens every fifth slightly — place the tempered fifth (in cents):
config.why: 700 cents instead of a pure 702 — the error spread evenly, so every key sounds equally, modestly in tune.

activities.anchor: the tuning note A = 440 Hz is a law of nature
activities.caption: true or false — pitch standards
activities.name: smPitchJudge

statements.s: A = 440 Hz is a convention standardised by the International Organization for Standardization in 1955.
statements.why: ISO 16, chosen partly to suit orchestras and instruments — politics with a tuning fork.

statements.s: Baroque ensembles often tune to A ≈ 415 Hz.
statements.why: And orchestras have drifted upward for brightness.

statements.s: 440 Hz is fixed by the physics of the ear.
statements.why: It is a convention — pitch standards are politics with a tuning fork.

statements.s: The octave itself (2:1) is the interval every musical culture treats as 'the same note, higher'.
statements.why: The one universal interval — while the standard pitched around it moves with committees.

activities.anchor: is the sense that one note
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the cadence analysis
activities.name: smCadenceSpot

config.prompt: A student's programme-note analysis contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The primary chords I, IV and V can harmonise almost any folk melody.
The dominant seventh's added fourth note creates a dissonance that demands resolution to the tonic.
The plagal cadence IV–I is the full stop of music.
Modulation usually moves to a related key so the ear follows.
config.correction: The perfect cadence V–I is the full stop; IV–I (plagal) is the gentle amen.
config.why: Chords become cadences, the punctuation of music — and every punctuation mark has its own weight.

activities.anchor: Italian publishers dominated early printed music
activities.caption: call the magnitude — allegro's engine speed
activities.name: smTempoEstimate

config.prompt: Allegro — 'fast' — sits at roughly what speed (BPM)?
config.why: Allegro runs roughly 120–156 BPM, between andante (walking, ~76–108) and presto (168+).
config.context: The names are Italian because Italian publishers dominated early printed music.

activities.anchor: Texture describes the fabric of simultaneous activity
activities.caption: drag the divider — one line versus many
activities.name: smTextureCompare

config.prompt: Texture counts independent melodic lines, not sound sources — drag the divider between the two cases:

before.label: A crowd in unison
before.text: One unaccompanied line — monophonic, however many people sing it: a lone chanter, a whistled tune, a crowd in unison.

after.label: The round's second voice
after.text: When the second voice of 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat' enters, you are in polyphony — two or more independent melodies of equal importance.

config.why: Monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, heterophonic are the fabrics — count the lines, not the headcount.
